analysis.one_liner: Entitles nearly all families with children under 6 to subsidized child care, capping costs and raising provider pay.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 27, 2023 with 42 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal entitlement to child care for children under 6 whose parents work, look for work, train, or study. Families at or below 85% of their state's median income would pay nothing; families above that would pay no more than 7% of income. The federal government would pay providers rates high enough to cover their real costs, including living wages for staff, and would pour money into starting and expanding child care programs. It was funded as an open-ended mandatory program through fiscal 2029.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who pay among the highest child care costs in the world, and the child care workforce, whose pay would rise to match that of elementary educators with similar credentials. Child care providers gain a guaranteed, cost-covering payment stream plus startup, quality, and facilities grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible child under 6 in a participating state would be entitled to child care assistance beginning October 1, 2024, covering parents who work, are self-employed, search for work, train, study, or are in treatment or leave.

Families with income at or below 85% of state median income would pay no copayment at all; copayments above that are capped at no more than 7% of family income, and providers would be barred from charging families more than the subsidy plus the copayment.

State payment rates would have to be set from a cost-estimation model so providers can fully cover their costs, including adequate wages for all staff — at minimum a living wage, and wages equivalent to similarly credentialed elementary educators — adjusted annually for cost of living.

The bill appropriates $20 billion for grants to localities in states that do not participate and for Head Start expansion, plus $1.3 billion for federal administration, and a second title provides ongoing base grants to providers with at least 70% of subgrant funds required to go to staff wages, cost-of-living raises, and benefits.

Providers would receive startup and supply-expansion grants, quality grants, and facilities grants, prioritized for underserved communities, and existing providers who accept subsidies would be deemed eligible for a transition period.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended mandatory appropriations for fiscal 2024–2029 on top of existing child care funding, which states would be required to maintain.

drawbacks.text: The core program is funded with 'such sums as may be necessary' for each of fiscal 2024 through 2029 — an open-ended, uncapped federal entitlement whose total cost depends entirely on participation, not a fixed budget.

Because state payment rates must guarantee living wages and educator-equivalent pay for provider staff, the federal government would effectively set pay levels across the child care sector through its funding conditions.
Even families above 150% of state median income would receive subsidized care, with their cost capped at 7% of income, so higher-income households benefit too.

Providers would face new licensing pathways, tiered quality systems, and wage requirements; existing subsidized providers have only about 3.5 years of transition before needing to meet the full standards, and smaller home-based providers could struggle with the compliance load.
Expanding a universal entitlement while the supply of child care slots and workers is fixed risks a period where demand outruns available care, unless the supply-building grants scale up quickly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families with young children, the benefit is direct and large: child care costs in many places exceed what families pay for housing, and this bill eliminates or sharply caps those costs while also addressing the sector's chronic low wages. The cost side is serious and honest supporters would concede it: this is a major new open-ended federal entitlement, effectively a public funding commitment to the entire child care sector's cost structure, with the federal government shaping wages and quality standards nationwide. The design is thoughtful about supply, wages, and transition, but the bill never says what the program costs in total, and that open-endedness is a legitimate reason fiscal skeptics would balk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never reached the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced S. 1354 on April 27, 2023, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
The bill had 42 cosponsors: 40 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 2 of its 4 independents, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer; no Republican signed on.

The bill text lays out a birth-through-five child care entitlement with no copayments for most families, cost-covering provider payment rates, wage requirements for child care staff, and grant programs to expand supply.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself, since it died in committee. The outcome preserves the status quo: child care costs stay where they are, falling directly on working families, and child care workers remain among the lowest-paid part of the education workforce. The sector avoids new wage mandates and compliance requirements, and no one has to find funding for the open-ended program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The child care status quo; costs stay on families

industries.industry: Child care providers (centers and home-based programs)
industries.note: The bill routes all child care assistance through licensed providers, guarantees them payment rates that fully cover their costs, and adds startup, quality, and facilities grants — making them the permanent public channel for child care funding. Their interest runs alongside families here: both gain from the new money.

Payment rates must fund a living wage for all provider staff and wages equivalent to similarly credentialed elementary educators, and at least 70% of the new base grants must go to wages, raises, and benefits. Child care is one of the lowest-paying education jobs, so this is a direct pay increase tied to public funding.
The bill appropriates $20 billion that can fund Head Start expansion in states that do not participate, with priority for underserved populations.
